intro: Installing a wet room in Borthwickhouse is one of the more involved bathroom projects you can take on, and it's not something to rush into without proper planning. Whether you're adapting a bathroom for accessibility reasons, modernising an older home, or simply want a sleek, open shower space, a wet room done properly transforms how a bathroom feels and functions. The challenge here, as with many properties in this part of Midlothian, is that the buildings themselves often have quirks — thick stone walls, uneven floors, or limited drainage options — that make a wet room installation more complex than a standard bathroom refit. Getting the waterproofing and fall right from the start is everything.
localContext: Borthwickhouse sits in a quiet corner of Midlothian, and its housing stock reflects that mix of old and newer Scotland you find throughout the area. Many homes here are older stone-built properties with solid walls and floors that have shifted and settled over decades. Period cottages in and around Borthwickhouse often have quarry-tiled or suspended timber floors, neither of which is straightforward when it comes to laying the tanked, fully waterproofed screed a wet room demands. Modern estate homes, by contrast, tend to have more predictable construction and can be easier to work with — but even these need a specialist eye on drainage gradients and waste routes. Borthwickhouse also sits in a moderately hard water area, which is worth bearing in mind when choosing your shower fittings, screen glass, and tiling grout. Limescale builds up over time on unprotected surfaces, so specifying the right sealants and considering a water softener or descaling filter for the shower head will save you a lot of maintenance headaches further down the line.
serviceDetail: A professional wet room installation in Borthwickhouse typically follows a clear sequence, though the exact process varies depending on your property type. The first stage is a proper survey — a good installer will assess the existing floor structure, check where the soil stack runs, and confirm that the fall to the drain can be achieved without raising the floor height excessively. In older stone-built properties, this sometimes means cutting into a solid floor to reposition drainage; in period cottages with timber floors, it may involve adding a structural subfloor layer before any waterproofing work begins. Once the prep is complete, the waterproofing system — usually a tanking membrane applied to all walls and the floor — is installed. This is the most critical part of the job and where shortcuts cause serious long-term damage. After tanking, the screed is laid with the correct gradient towards the drain, typically around 1 in 80. Tiling or stone cladding follows, along with fitting the shower valve, screen or glass panel, and any heated towel rails or underfloor heating elements. In Borthwickhouse homes with older plumbing, this is also a good point to update supply pipework, particularly if you're moving to a thermostatic shower valve. The whole process, from start to a usable wet room, usually takes five to eight working days for a standard bathroom-sized space.
pricing: In Borthwickhouse, wet room installations typically fall in the range of £6,500 to £12,000, depending on several factors. The size of the space, the complexity of the drainage work, and the condition of the existing floor structure are the biggest variables. Older stone-built properties and period cottages often sit at the higher end because of the additional groundwork needed before waterproofing can begin. The cost of materials — particularly wall and floor tiles, the shower valve, and any heated flooring — also varies widely based on specification. A mid-range, well-specified wet room in a Borthwickhouse home of average size will generally come in around £7,500 to £9,000 all in, including labour, materials, and waste removal.
whyLocal: Choosing a tradesperson who knows Borthwickhouse and the surrounding Midlothian area genuinely makes a difference with a job like this. Local installers will have worked in similar stone-built properties and older cottages nearby and will understand the common structural quirks — things like lime mortar walls that need specific primers, or drainage routes that aren't where you'd expect them. They're also more invested in the quality of the finished result because their reputation is built locally. On a job with as much riding on the waterproofing as a wet room, that local accountability matters. You're also more likely to get someone who can revisit easily if a small snag needs sorting after the job is done.

faqs.q: Can a wet room be installed in a period cottage in Borthwickhouse with a timber floor?
faqs.a: Yes, but it requires more preparation than a solid floor. The timber subfloor typically needs to be reinforced or overlaid with a rigid cement board before the tanking membrane is applied. A good installer will assess the joist depth and existing floor build-up to work out the most practical approach without raising the floor height to an awkward level.

faqs.q: How does the moderately hard water in Borthwickhouse affect a wet room?
faqs.a: Hard water leaves limescale deposits on glass screens, tile grout, and shower fittings over time. Specifying a quality grout sealer, using polished or large-format tiles with fewer grout lines, and fitting a descaling filter on the shower are all practical steps. Some homeowners in the area also install an inline water softener, which significantly reduces the ongoing maintenance burden.

faqs.q: How long does a wet room installation take in a typical Borthwickhouse home?
faqs.a: For a standard bathroom-sized wet room, most installations take between five and eight working days from strip-out to completion. Stone-built or older properties in Borthwickhouse can add a day or two if drainage repositioning or additional floor preparation is needed. Your installer should give you a realistic timeline after the initial survey, not just a best-case estimate.

faqs.q: Is planning permission needed to install a wet room in Borthwickhouse?
faqs.a: In most cases, no — wet room installation is considered permitted development for domestic properties. However, if your home is a listed building or sits within a designated area, you may need to check with Midlothian Council before starting work. It's worth confirming this early, particularly for older stone-built properties, as some in this part of Scotland do carry conservation restrictions.
